content: Scrapie is a fatal and progressive neurodegenerative disease that affects the central nervous systems of sheep and goats. It belongs to a group of diseases known as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs), which also include bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE, commonly referred to as mad cow disease) and chronic wasting disease in deer. Similar to other TSEs, scrapie is believed to be caused by prions, which are misfolded proteins capable of inducing abnormal folding in normal proteins. The disease has been recognized since the 18th century, with the first documented case in 1732. Importantly, scrapie does not appear to be transmissible to humans. The name scrapie originates from one of its hallmark symptoms, where affected animals compulsively scrape their fleece against objects such as rocks, trees, or fences. This behavior is thought to be driven by an intense itching sensation. Other clinical signs of scrapie include excessive lip-smacking, abnormal gaits, and episodes of convulsive collapse. Scrapie is both infectious and transmissible among sheep and goats. Because there is no cure for the disease, one of the primary methods of control involves quarantining and culling affected animals. However, the disease often persists within flocks and can even arise spontaneously in flocks with no prior history of infection. The exact mechanisms of transmission between animals and other aspects of the disease's biology remain poorly understood, making this an active area of scientific research. Recent studies suggest that prions may be excreted in urine and can remain viable in the environment for decades, further complicating eradication efforts. In the United Kingdom, the government has implemented a National Scrapie Plan, which promotes selective breeding of sheep that are genetically more resistant to the disease. This program aims to reduce the prevalence of scrapie within the UK sheep population over time. Scrapie is known to occur in Europe and North America, but Australia and New Zealand, both major sheep-producing nations, remain free of the disease. A diagnostic test is now available, which involves sampling a small amount of lymphatic tissue from the third eyelid of the animal. This test has improved the ability to detect and manage the disease. In response to concerns about BSE, many European countries have banned certain traditional sheep and goat products that are made without removing the spinal cord, such as smalahove and smokie, to minimize potential risks.
